issues.legal_issue: A creditor’s winding-up petition must be refused where the company raises a bona fide, substantial dispute about the alleged debt and adduces prima facie evidence supporting its defence.
material_facts: The company disputed most of the claimed debts in fact and law, relying on lack of privity, limitation and the absence of the alleged transactions from its books.
The company produced prima facie evidence supporting those defences, including a receipt showing that one claimed invoice had been paid.
The company acknowledged a smaller amount in its books but asserted that the parties had agreed to a reduced settlement payable from the proceeds of a machinery sale.
issues.conclusion: The claims were bona fide disputed and supported by substantial defences, so the winding-up order was properly refused.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 433(c) of the Companies Act, 1956, a company is not to be wound up on a creditor’s petition where the debt is bona fide disputed and the defence is substantial. The defence must be in good faith and of substance, likely to succeed in law, and supported by prima facie proof of its factual basis. The Court relied on Amalgamated Commercial Traders (P.) Ltd. v. A. C. K. Krishnaswami, London & Paris Banking Corporation, Re Brighton Club & Norfolk Hotel Co. Ltd., Re A. Company and Re Tweeds Garages Ltd. Where the debt is undisputed, an assertion that the company can pay but chooses not to pay does not defeat the petition; where only the precise amount of an otherwise-established debt is disputed, a winding-up order may still be made.

predicates.creditor_winding_up_petition: A creditor has petitioned for the company to be wound up.
predicates.bona_fide_substantial_debt_dispute: The company disputes the alleged debt in good faith on a substantial factual or legal basis.
predicates.prima_facie_evidence_supports_defence: The company produces prima facie evidence supporting the facts on which its defence depends.

issues.definition: When a creditor seeks winding up, a good-faith substantial dispute supported by prima facie evidence results in refusal of winding up on the disputed debt.

issues.legal_issue: The court may refuse a creditor’s winding-up petition when creditors oppose winding up for reasonable grounds and the order would not benefit the petitioner or creditors generally.
material_facts: Creditors holding claims aggregating a substantial amount supported the company and resisted the petition.
The company proposed using the proceeds from the machinery sale to pursue other business within its objects, with support from a major creditor.
issues.conclusion: The opposition of the supporting creditors was a relevant reason for refusing the winding-up order.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 557 of the Companies Act, 1956, the court may ascertain the wishes of creditors in winding-up matters and may, for good reason, refuse an order despite a petitioner’s claimed right to one. The court tests whether the opposition is reasonable and whether there are matters requiring investigation in a winding up; it will not make an order on a creditor’s petition if the order would not benefit that creditor or creditors generally. The Court relied on Re P. & J. Macrae Ltd.

rule.if: creditor_winding_up_petition and substantial_creditors_oppose_winding_up and opposition_has_reasonable_basis and winding_up_would_not_benefit_creditors

predicates.creditor_winding_up_petition: A creditor has petitioned for the company to be wound up.
predicates.substantial_creditors_oppose_winding_up: Creditors representing substantial claims oppose the winding up.
predicates.opposition_has_reasonable_basis: The opposing creditors have a reasonable basis for preferring that the company continue rather than be wound up.
predicates.winding_up_would_not_benefit_creditors: A winding-up order would not benefit the petitioner or the creditors generally.

issues.definition: If substantial creditors reasonably oppose winding up and the order would not benefit creditors, the court may refuse the petition.

issues.legal_issue: A machinery sale approved by shareholders and supported by the petitioners is not shown to be unauthorised or improvident merely because the petitioners later challenge it.
material_facts: The petitioners, while directors and shareholders, attended a board meeting at which the machinery sale was approved.
They later wrote that they had no objection to the sale, and the company’s shareholders unanimously approved it.
The petitioners were parties to the proposed sale and had themselves sought to buy the machinery.
issues.conclusion: The machinery sale could not be treated as unauthorised or improvident on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: The court considered the sale within the province of company management and treated shareholder approval, together with the petitioners’ own consent and participation, as inconsistent with the contention that the sale was unauthorised or improvident. No earlier case or statutory provision is identified for this ruling.

predicates.creditor_winding_up_petition_challenges_: A creditor seeking winding up relies on a company asset sale as an allegedly unauthorised or improvident transaction.
predicates.shareholders_approved_sale: The company’s shareholders approved the asset sale.
predicates.petitioners_supported_or_participated_in: The petitioners consented to, supported, or participated in the proposed sale.

issues.definition: When a winding-up petitioner challenges an asset sale that shareholders approved and the petitioner supported or participated in, the sale is not shown to be unauthorised or improvident.

issues.legal_issue: Trading losses and the sale of the company’s principal machinery do not establish that its substratum has disappeared where there remains a reasonable prospect of profitable business within its objects.
material_facts: The company had incurred substantial trading losses and proposed selling its machinery.
The company stated that it intended to use the proceeds for other profitable business within its objects, including export and yarn-related business.
A major creditor was prepared to assist the company in pursuing that business, and the company had not abandoned its business objects.
issues.conclusion: The company’s substratum had not disappeared.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding whether a company’s substratum has gone, the court considers the company’s objects and its case on the prospect of future business. Trading losses alone do not destroy the substratum unless there is no reasonable prospect of future profit, and the court is reluctant to infer that no such prospect exists. The Court relied on Re Suburban Hotel Co. and Davis & Co. v. Brunswick (Australia) Ltd.

predicates.creditor_winding_up_petition_alleges_sub: A creditor’s winding-up petition alleges that the company’s substratum has disappeared.
predicates.company_has_not_abandoned_its_objects: The company has not abandoned the business objects for which it was formed.
predicates.reasonable_prospect_of_future_profit: The company has a reasonable prospect of carrying on profitable business in the future.

issues.definition: Despite an allegation that the substratum is lost, it is not shown to have disappeared if the company retains its objects and a reasonable prospect of future profit.

issues.legal_issue: A company is not shown to be unable to pay its debts where it can meet admitted creditors’ claims, continues business and has resources, even though its financial position is disputed.
material_facts: The company had not ceased carrying on business and had resources and prospects for future business.
It deposited the disputed claims in court as directed.
The Court found that the company had not been shown to be unable to meet the outstandings of its admitted creditors.
issues.conclusion: The company was not shown to be unable to pay its admitted debts, and the alleged financial shortfall did not justify winding up on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 433(c) of the Companies Act, 1956 concerns inability to pay debts. On the facts, the company’s continued business, resources, prospects and deposit of the disputed claims meant that inability to meet admitted creditors’ claims was not established.

predicates.creditor_winding_up_petition_alleges_ina: A creditor’s winding-up petition alleges that the company cannot pay its debts.
predicates.admitted_creditors_can_be_paid: The company is able to meet the claims of creditors whose debts are admitted.
predicates.company_continues_business_with_resource: The company continues business and has resources or prospects with which to meet its obligations.

issues.definition: When a creditor alleges inability to pay but admitted creditors can be paid and the company continues business with resources, inability to pay is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A creditor’s winding-up petition may be rejected as an improper use of the process when it is brought to coerce the company over groundless claims rather than for a legitimate winding-up purpose.
material_facts: The petitioners had been directors and knew the company’s affairs, but made no demand for the alleged debts while they were involved in its management.
They sold their shares and left management, then presented the petition when the machinery sale was about to be completed, despite having previously supported that sale.
The Court found that the petitioners’ claims were disputed and that the circumstances indicated an improper motive.
issues.conclusion: The petition was not presented for a legitimate purpose, and the circumstances supported treating it as an improper use of the winding-up process.
issues.legal_principle: A winding-up petition is not a legitimate means of coercing a company into satisfying groundless claims. The Court relied on Mann & Anr. v. Goldstein & Anr., in which prosecution of a winding-up petition based on substantially disputed debts was restrained as an abuse of process.

predicates.creditor_winding_up_petition: A creditor has petitioned for the company to be wound up.
predicates.claims_are_groundless_or_substantially_d: The claims used to support the petition are groundless or substantially disputed.
predicates.petitioners_use_winding_up_to_coerce_pay: The petitioners use the winding-up process to pressure the company into paying those claims.

issues.definition: A creditor’s petition based on groundless or substantially disputed claims and used to coerce payment is not a legitimate winding-up purpose.
